name: basten
author: animals-and-nature agent
description:
basten v4 (direction: animals and nature) -- A FISH TANK: THE FISH THAT SWIM OVER AND NIBBLE THE TOP
OFF A WEED. PRIVATE; never shown to players. Earlier versions: basten.v1.json (7 %), basten.v2.json
(33 % under the old 6-round format, then 0 %/0 % in the first 7-class run), basten.v3.json (0 %
without a demo for six Opus players, 30 % with one over four).

WHY v4. v3 put the object in the clue (an empty tank with weeds) and asked for the same picture with
fish added, N of them nose-on-a-weed. The clue therefore showed the ANSWER'S SHAPE but the caption
was a FREE PARAMETER: "how many fish to draw" cannot be checked against a harvested clue, so no
hypothesis could be falsified offline and every one cost a slice of a round. Both players in
`lad-kelmar-v3-1` say so in their notes: they spent their demos on the classes whose EDIT TYPE they
could not name (virel, fennick, kelmar) and left the "canvas" classes undemoed, because the answer's
shape was already obvious. basten then scored 0/790 and 0/497. kelmar1a's post-mortem: "N (3..5) is
independent of the picture (all 9 combinations of N x water-depth occur, max plant height is always
3), so it is not a height, a depth or a count of anything visible. 15 rules tried, 0/790." The rule
was findable; nothing in the clue could test it.

v4 does to basten what v3 did to fennick and kelmar: THE FISH ARE ALREADY IN THE TANK, and the
answer is that picture with the fish that nibble moved and the weeds they nibble made shorter. The
caption counts the edits ("2 nibble"), so a team can test any candidate rule against ~70 harvested
clues in round 1 for free -- the fennick/kelmar checksum, which every player in the last two runs
called the best design feature in the pool.

THE CLUE is a finished picture of a tank, 30-40 columns wide:
  line 1  the water surface, "~" repeated W times
  D rows  the water (D = 5 or 6): "." is open water, "|" is a segment of a weed, and the fish are
          drawn "><>" (swimming right, nose on the right) and "<><" (swimming left, nose on the
          left), three cells of one row, never on a weed, never touching another fish
  line    the gravel bed, "#" repeated W times
  line    the caption "<n> nibble"
Every weed grows out of the gravel and fills the bottom h rows of its own column, h = 2..D-1;
weeds are 5-9 columns apart, never in the outer two columns, one of them always reaches the top
water row and one is always exactly 2 tall. 5-8 fish. Clue <= 336 chars.

THE RULE, the sentence a kid says while pointing: EACH FISH SWIMS OVER TO THE WEED IT IS LOOKING
STRAIGHT AT AND NIBBLES THE TOP OFF -- IF IT CAN REACH THE TOP. Formally, a fish nibbles iff
(a) looking straight ahead of its nose along its own row, the first thing that is not open water is
a weed (a fish in the way stops it; so does the glass), and (b) that weed's topmost segment is in
the fish's own row or one row above it. The edit for each nibbling fish: the fish slides along its
row until its nose is in the cell next to the weed (the cells it leaves become open water), and the
weed's TOPMOST segment becomes open water -- the weed is one shorter and still grows from the
gravel, because a fish cannot bite a hole in the middle and leave the top floating. Nothing else
changes. The caption counts the nibbling fish, which is exactly the number of edits.

The generator guarantees the two things that make the caption a clean checksum: no clue fish starts
with its nose already against a weed (so every nibble is a visible move), and no fish is ever left
staring at a weed through another fish in a position where it would matter -- the "something in the
way" half of the rule is drawn, never load-bearing.

ANSWER = that picture edited. The caption line may be kept or dropped (house rule). The scorer
reads both pictures with .split(), so indentation, blank lines, trailing spaces and CRLF are free;
the answer is UNIQUE, so a shotgun of several candidate pictures in one answer scores 0.

A DEMO AS IT RENDERS (seed 400021, n = 2):

  clue                                answer
  ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~      ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
  .....................<><......      .....................<><......
  .......................|......      .......................|......
  .......................|......      .......................|......
  ......<><..|....><>....|...<><      ......<><.......><>....|...<><
  ...|..><>..|.....|.....|..<><.      ........><>|.....|.....|..<><.
  ...|...<><.|.....|.....|..<><.      ...|<><....|.....|.....|..<><.
  ##############################      ##############################
  2 nibble                            2 nibble

Two fish nibble. The "><>" in the second water row from the bottom was three cells short of the
weed at column 11 whose tip is one row above it: it slides up to the weed and that tip is gone. The
"<><" in the bottom row does the same to the little weed at column 3. Everything else stays where
it is, and the picture says why: FOUR fish are looking straight at the tall weed at column 23 --
two of them in the same rows as the nibblers, one of them closer to its weed than either nibbler --
and its top is two, three and four rows above them, out of reach. One more fish ("<><" in row 4)
has a weed behind its tail, not in front of its nose.

THE FOOTHOLD (lever 7). 12.1 % of clues say "0 nibble" -- nobody is looking at a weed it can reach
-- and the correct answer IS the clue echoed back. A team with only the format banks those, exactly
fennick's floor, and learns from the caption that the class is picture-graded rather than
exact-match.

WHAT EVERY DEMO SHOWS (4000 clues). At least one fish that is looking straight at a weed and cannot
reach the top: 100 % (two or more: 94.1 %). A fish with a weed behind its tail: 100 %. A fish
nowhere near a weed: 53.9 %. A weed nobody touches: 100 %. On the clues with a nibble: a bite one
row above the fish 93.8 %, a bite level with the fish 45.8 %, a nibbler and an out-of-reach fish in
the SAME ROW 86.4 %, an out-of-reach fish higher in the tank than a nibbler 78.4 %, one nearer its
weed than a nibbler 79.9 %, one further away than a nibbler 79.2 %. Those last three are deliberate:
they stop "the n fish nearest the surface / nearest their weed / furthest from it" from being the
rule by accident.

WITNESS TABLE (4000 fresh clues; every attacker except the echoes knows the drawing convention and
the caption, i.e. it models a player who has seen a demo and holds the wrong rule).
  the TRUE rule (solve)                                        100.0 %
  the true rule with the caption dropped                       100.0 %
  only the short weeds get nibbled                              31.4 %
  the n facing fish furthest from their weed                    26.2 %
  the n facing fish closest to their weed                       24.9 %
  n random facing fish                                          24.9 %
  the n facing fish nearest the surface                         24.4 %
  swim over, but bite the segment level with the fish           18.1 %
  only the fish level with the top nibble (reach nothing)       18.1 %
  n random fish, either way round                               16.6 %
  swim over, weed untouched  <- the natural blind reading       12.8 %
  the top eaten but the fish stays where it is                  12.8 %
  swim over, bottom segment eaten / whole weed eaten            12.8 %
  the clue echoed unchanged (the foothold)                      12.8 %
  the clue echoed with the caption dropped                      12.8 %
  reach two rows instead of one                                  2.8 %
  every fish facing a weed nibbles                               0.0 %
  previous clue's answer replayed / one fixed answer            0.0 %
  all fish deleted / empty / junk / caption alone / rows alone   0.0 %
  shotgun (the answer twice), rows reversed, row duplicated      0.0 %
Nothing insight-free beats 31 %, and 12.8 of every one of those points is the n = 0 echo. The 18-31 %
band is the intended partial tier: a player who has the picture grammar and the render but the wrong
half of the reach clause. Note the three ranking heuristics (nearest the surface / nearest the weed /
furthest from it) all sit at ~25 %: the generator decorrelates depth and distance from reach on
purpose, because in an earlier build "the n topmost facing fish" scored 83 %.

THE OFFLINE CHECKSUM (why the caption is the whole design). For each rival law, how often its own
count agrees with the caption on a harvested clue: every fish facing a weed 0.0 %, reach two rows
3.1 %, only weeds 3+ tall 5.5 %, only the bottom-row fish 11.8 %, reach nothing (level only) 16.9 %,
only weeds shorter than 3 30.8 %, the true rule 100 %. So a team that enumerates "which fish does
the caption count?" laws at all kills the whole field in round 1 against ~5 clues without answering
anything -- and the surviving laws that fit the count by construction (any "n of the facing fish"
tie-break) are killed by one demo, which shows a nibbler and an out-of-reach fish side by side in
the same row 86 % of the time. The difficulty is entirely in asking how far the fish has to reach.

INTENDED DISCOVERY PATH. (1) The clue is unmistakably a fish tank; the caption names the verb and
counts the edits, so the answer's shape is free. (2) Round 1 harvest: the count is not the fish
count, not the weed count, not the number of fish beside a weed; it IS the number of fish with a
weed straight ahead of them -- minus some. (3) The demo shows what an edit is (the fish moved; the
weed lost its tip) and, beside it, a fish that did not move although it is looking at a weed. (4)
The lateral step is vertical: how far above the fish is the top it is going to bite? One row, no
more. A kid says "he can't reach that one" in one look; the model's default hypotheses are all
horizontal (nearest, leftmost, blocked, which weed) and all sit at 25 %.

VALIDATION. quickcheck --seeds 200: OK, one warning -- "score accepts the clue itself as a
solution", which is the n = 0 foothold and is meant to be there (fennick and kelmar have the same).
10 000 random 32-bit seeds: generate deterministic, 10 000/10 000 distinct clues, no fallback, mean
0.38 ms / p99 0.95 ms / worst 4.5 ms (cap 100); 4-9 fish and 4-6 weeds per tank; clue 225-336 chars,
solution the same. solve() scores 1 on 10 000/10 000, mean 0.019 ms (cap 2000). score: 484 chars
(cap 512), mean 0.020 ms, 0.019 ms on 4000 chars of junk (cap 50), always 0 or 1. Scorer cross-checked against an independent re-implementation
written from this prose (explicit column walk, no regex) on 50 000 (clue, answer) pairs -- shipped
demos plus 24 structural mutations each -- with 0 disagreements. Junk: 12 000 random strings over
the picture alphabet plus every prefix and suffix of every clue: 0 raises, 0 non-binary returns, 0
false positives (bar the n = 0 echoes, which are correct answers). Lenient, all 100 %: caption kept
or dropped, caption count altered, blank lines, indentation, right-padded rows, CRLF. Strict, all
0 %: rows reversed, surface or gravel row dropped, a water row duplicated or taken from the clue
where it should have changed, the picture shifted one column, fish flipped, an extra fish, a fish
deleted, a weed segment restored, a second weed tip eaten, the answer twice.

LEVERS. Too easy (the likeliest overshoot is a player who reads "reach" as "the weed the fish is
level with"): make the reach depend on which way the fish is swimming, or let the bite take the top
TWO segments off a weed taller than 3. Too hard: raise the share of clues whose nibble is level with
the fish (currently 45.8 %) so the vertical dimension is visible in more demos, or draw one weed
already nibbled in the clue as a worked instance. The rule is one clause and the picture is 5/5 on
object recognition, so the softening lever of last resort is the caption: "<n> reach" instead of
"<n> nibble" points straight at the clause.

Design notes and the full iteration record: challenges/lab/NOTES_nature.md.
solve:
def solve(clue):
    L = clue.split("\n")
    P = [list(x) for x in L[1:-2]]
    W = len(L[0])
    for i in range(len(P)):
        r = "".join(P[i])
        for m in re.finditer("><>|<><", r):
            a = m.start()
            d = 1 if r[a] == ">" else -1
            j = a + 3 if d > 0 else a - 1
            while 0 <= j < W and r[j] == ".":            # a weed straight ahead?
                j += d
            if 0 <= j < W and r[j] == "|":
                t = [x[j] for x in P].index("|")         # where its top is
                if i - t < 2:                            # near enough to reach
                    b = j - 3 if d > 0 else j + 1        # swim right up to it
                    P[i][a:a + 3] = list("...")
                    P[i][b:b + 3] = list(r[a:a + 3])
                    P[t][j] = "."                        # and nibble the top off
    return "\n".join([L[0]] + ["".join(x) for x in P] + [L[-2], L[-1]])
